item.title: Push-based CDC into Unity Catalog with Zerobus Ingest and Debezium
item.abstract: Data in operational databases drives business decisions, and much of that analysis happens in the lakehouse. Getting the data there is hard when the database sits in a private corporate network, a customer-controlled environment or a restricted subnet whose network policies block inbound connections from external services. Many teams need their PostgreSQL changes in Databricks, but the team that owns the database also wants to own the capture. That team runs the process that reads the write-ahead log and decides which connections leave its network. On the other side, the changes land in governed Delta tables that pipelines and analysts can build on. Debezium is a common open source tool that teams can own the full deployment to extract a change data capture feed from a database. It sits next to the database, reads its write-ahead log and pushes events outward. Zerobus Ingest is the destination, a push interface that writes records directly into Unity Catalog Delta tables. The open-source Debezium Server Zerobus sink joins the two without the use of a traditional Kafka cluster between capture and the lakehouse. Engineers at NVIDIA and Databricks teamed up to build this sink and contributed it to the open-source Debezium project. Databricks built the typed Zerobus Ingest sink. Then, NVIDIA contributed envelope mode, which lands the full Debezium change event, along with the delivery safeguards around it, such as idempotency keys and durable acknowledgment before source offsets advance. The Zerobus Ingest sink is shipped in the Debezium Server 3.7 release . This post covers what Debezium and Zerobus each do, the raw change envelope NVIDIA contributed to the sink, and how landed events become current-state or historical tables. For a hands-on walkthrough, including a live run from a local PostgreSQL table to a current-state table, see the companion how-to blog on the Databricks Community . Replicating operational database changes into the lakehouse reliably has to solve several problems at once: Given those requirements, we need to start with the architecture of which data would flow from source to sink. In this blog, we’ll explore a traditional message bus architecture compared to an architecture using Zerobus Ingest. Architecture with a Message bus: In many enterprise environments, outbound connectivity from inside a perimeter is far easier to permit than inbound access. When your team wants to run a deployment of the change feed extracting agent, a local push model lets data flow outwards to a destination. In a traditional setup, this would be a message bus such as Kafka. Running Kafka requires resources for capacity planning to predict the number of brokers needed to handle peak load for physical scaling and to estimate the number of partitions for logical scaling, which consumers need to keep up with the rate of production. This requires a dedicated team with experience in this Kafka deployment and management. Once the data lands in Kafka, you have the next job to fulfill, which is to replicate those events to the lakehouse. This could be through a deployment of ingestion jobs such as with Spark, Kafka Connector, or other tooling. The result is a two-hop architecture from Debezium to the lakehouse. Architecture with Zerobus Ingest: When your sole destination is the lakehouse, Zerobus allows you to bypass intermediate hops such as the message bus. This both streamlines your end-to-end architecture and eliminates the need to deploy and manage Kafka infrastructure for data transit. When using Zerobus as a sink with Debezium it continues to work during your peak hours, without tuning. Debezium is an open-source, log-based change data capture platform. Rather than polling tables, it reads a database's transaction log, for example, PostgreSQL's write-ahead log (WAL), MySQL's binlog, and MongoDB's change streams. It then emits each change as a structured event. The project began in 2015, and today supports a broad connector ecosystem (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB, and more). Each change event carries a consistent envelope: Debezium adds minimal load to the primary database due to its log tailing as opposed to polling to capture changes at low latency, and preserves commit ordering. Debezium has two operating models. One which runs on Kafka Connect, and the other which is a “stand-alone server” which can be stood up on vanilla compute. Plugin inside a Kafka Connect cluster Standalone Quarkus application Apache Kafka (then sink out to other systems) Directly to non-Kafka targets via a sink adapter. (Like Zerobus Ingest) Kafka is your canonical event bus; you want Connect's distributed workers, SMTs, schema registry You don't run Kafka, or you want to push CDC directly to a purpose-built destination Debezium Server , the standalone runtime, serves as your source-side agent that tails transaction logs and sends change events directly to Databricks’ Zerobus Ingest, without a Kafka cluster serving as the transport. So we have identified Debezium as our log tailer. Now we need to get the events into Databricks. Zerobus Ingest is a serverless, push-based ingestion service that writes data directly into Unity Catalog–governed Delta tables, with no message broker to run. Producers connect to a Zerobus endpoint and stream records that land in an open-format Delta table. It's built to handle high throughput, highly concurrent workloads. By skipping the step of a message broker, we are able to simplify the architecture, and the maintenance of having to scale and run ingestion pipelines to move the data to the lakehouse. Put together with Debezium, your CDC pipelines would look something like this: Zerobus Ingest is append-only. Once the change events land, the next step is to build a Type-1 dimensional table by performing a merge to obtain the latest version of each given primary key combination. The Zerobus sink in Debezium offers two table contracts. Typed mode, the default, maps each change event onto a table with the source’s own columns. Envelope mode, which NVIDIA contributed, lands the full Debezium change event in a fixed nine-column table: Records can be encoded as JSON (stored in VARIANT columns) or Protobuf. Envelope mode keeps the evidence downstream processing needs. source_position carries the source partition and offset, including the PostgreSQL LSN. idempotency_key is a SHA-256 identity of each event, derived from its destination, partition, key, operation and source position, so a redelivered event gets the same key. The key identifies events; it does not order them or deduplicate the table on its own. If a later group fails, an earlier durable group can be delivered again, so delivery is at-least-once and duplicates are handled downstream with idempotency_key . Envelope mode also filters by destination and operation, and rejects an oversized record before ingestion so its offset is never committed. Once CDC events land in Delta, a common medallion-style flow turns the raw change feed into something analysts and applications can use: Two ways to shape the change feed are worth naming briefly: The companion how-to blog on the Databricks Community walks through this end to end with a local PostgreSQL table. It configures Debezium Server with the Zerobus sink, checks an insert, update and delete in the envelope table, then builds the Type-1 (current-state) table with AUTO CDC, sequencing changes by source LSN. Choosing the right CDC architecture ultimately depends on your organization's networking constraints, operational preferences, and existing infrastructure.

item.title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics
item.abstract: It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscripts claiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip . After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next. Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science. On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “ nothing else really comparable ,” comparing the project to “ the famous Bourbaki books ,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century. Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory. The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code. Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound. Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work , while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits. For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it. That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code. “Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.” The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures . “We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said. To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.” Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own. The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said. Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.” Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply : “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.” Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code. Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does. “We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.” The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop. “You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.” Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”

OpenAI team states that Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. The update also adds GIF output, SVG export, markup-guided edits and a new complexity parameter. GPT-Image-2.6 is OpenAI’s image generation and editing model family for the API. It accepts text and image inputs and returns images. GPT-Image-2.6 Flare is built for fast iteration and interactive workflows. GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst is built for detailed compositions and editing. OpenAI states that Flare can generate images in as little as 6 seconds when quality is set to low. Sunburst targets higher quality and stronger consistency across edits at medium or high quality. ChatGPT users can now turn a prompt or a photo into an animated GIF. They can adjust animation speed, edit individual frames and share the result. If you omit it, both models use high. Low suits focused edits, such as changing a background or a sign. High helps with dense text, complex layouts and relationships between objects. OpenAI warns that higher complexity can add latency and introduce unwanted changes. Adjusting complexity has no separate fee. It is separate from quality , which controls rendering detail and fidelity. Image markup lets you mark up the exact region you want changed. The launch post says markup is coming to the API. The guide already lists markup-guided edits as supported for both models. It also lists SVG output and animated GIF output through the Image API. item.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent. Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call . Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”). The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs: Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy: The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel : your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity. Add Web Answer as a connector target. The connectorId tells the Gateway which managed integration to provision: in this case, an agent that searches the web and writes a cited answer. Outbound authentication is automatic for connectors. With GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE , the Gateway calls the Web Answer backend with the service role from Step 1, so you don’t create or store any credentials for the tool. Wait until get_gateway_target reports the target status as READY before you call it. As the Gateway administrator, you can also set a domain filter on the target. The filter applies to every call that goes through the target. To limit the target to a set of domains, set parameterValues to {"domainFilter": {"include": ["bis.org"], "exclude": ["unreliable-source.net"]}} . Your agent discovers Web Answer through the Gateway’s tools/list and calls it with tools/call , like any other MCP tool. This works with Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or any other MCP-compatible client. When a question needs current information, your agent calls the Web Answer tool ( web-answer-tool___WebAnswer ). Web Answer runs the agentic search and returns a finished answer with citations. Besides the question, the Web Answer tool takes optional arguments that your agent can set on each call: a domain filter to include or exclude sites, a published-date range, and a country to localize results. The agent’s domain filter is combined with the target’s filter. The agent can exclude more domains, or limit results to some of the target’s included domains, but it can’t add a domain that the target’s filter blocks. Web Answer returns an MCP tool result with both content and structuredContent fields. The answer is markdown text with inline citation markers like [ 1 ], and structuredContent.answer carries the same text alongside a structured citations list: structuredContent.answer normally holds a single block. Each citation carries the source url and, when available, the domain. Delete the Web Answer target when you no longer need it: If you created the Gateway only for this walkthrough, delete its targets first, then the Gateway (delete_gateway), and then the service role and its policy. There is no persistent infrastructure on the AWS side beyond these resources. After they are removed, you stop incurring charges. Web Answer inherits the same enterprise controls as other AgentCore tools: Web Answer helps agents retrieve current, cited information to support a range of knowledge-intensive workflows. Example scenarios include: Web Answer is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), with more AWS Regions coming soon. Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is priced at $10 per 1,000 tool calls. In this post, we showed how Web Answer gives your agents current, cited answers through agentic search, with no search pipeline for you to build or maintain. We granted a Gateway service role access to Web Answer, added a Web Answer target, called it from a Strands agent, and read the answer and its citations from the response. Use Web Search on AgentCore when your own model should reason over raw results, and Web Answer when your agent needs a finished, cited answer.

item.title: From Delta Sharing to OpenSharing: what changed, what's next
item.abstract: Delta Sharing has been the way thousands of organizations exchange live data across clouds and platforms without copying it. In June 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation announced that Delta Sharing has evolved into OpenSharing , an open, vendor-neutral protocol for sharing not just tables, but the broader set of assets that AI teams now depend on: agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data. If you already share data with Delta Sharing, or you're evaluating how to collaborate with partners on both data and AI assets, this post walks through what OpenSharing actually is, what's changed under the hood, and where the project is headed. When Databricks introduced Delta Sharing at Data + AI Summit 2021, the core problem it addressed was simple to state and hard to solve well: organizations wanted to share live data with partners, customers, and other teams, without exporting files, standing up brittle ETL jobs, or forcing every recipient onto the same platform. Delta Sharing was contributed to the Linux Foundation as an open protocol, built on Delta Lake and Parquet, so a provider could grant access to a table and a recipient could query it directly, in real time, from tools like Apache Spark, Power BI, Tableau, pandas, and many others. That open, zero-copy model resonated. Delta Sharing grew into the most widely adopted open protocol for secure data sharing, used by organizations including Amadeus, Atlassian, LSEG, SAP, Stripe, and The Trade Desk for cross-cloud and cross-platform collaboration, according to Databricks ( Databricks press release ). By the time Databricks announced OpenSharing in June 2026, Delta Sharing had reached more than 28,000 data recipients, with roughly a third of shares flowing across platforms through open connectors rather than staying inside Databricks-to-Databricks sharing ( Databricks blog ). Sharing had already grown well beyond tables. Through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, teams were exchanging views, volumes of unstructured files, notebooks, and registered ML models years before agents entered the picture, so structured data was never the whole story. What agents changed was the kind of asset that needed to move, and how far it needed to travel. Agent skills, the agents themselves, and the semantic context they run on all called for the same governed, zero-copy access that sharing had already proven out. Enterprises also wanted that access to reach across platforms and beyond Databricks-to-Databricks connections, and the open protocol still centered on tables, so these newer assets sat outside what open, cross-platform sharing could actually deliver. At the same time, enterprises kept asking for two related things: broader interoperability with formats like Apache Iceberg, and a way to bring data that lives on premises or in private clouds into the same governed sharing model, without migrating it first. Addressing both of these gaps meant rethinking Delta Sharing's scope, not just adding features to it. On June 10, 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation jointly announced OpenSharing as the next evolution of Delta Sharing ( Databricks press release , Linux Foundation press release ). Precision matters here, because OpenSharing operates at two distinct layers: The open ecosystem reaches beyond the protocol itself. Open source Unity Catalog, an Apache 2.0 project also governed under the Linux Foundation, provides a vendor-neutral catalog and governance layer for these assets, so a team can pair it with an open sharing server and run governed sharing entirely outside Databricks ( GitHub, Unity Catalog ). Databricks Co-founder and CTO Matei Zaharia framed the move this way: "Delta Sharing proved the industry would choose open over locked-in. OpenSharing extends that principle to the full AI stack, while expanding the cross-platform ecosystem to Iceberg recipients and on-premises providers" ( Databricks press release ). Linux Foundation CEO Jim Zemlin added that the goal is "a common, vendor-neutral framework that enables organizations to exchange AI assets securely and interoperably across platforms and ecosystems" ( Linux Foundation press release ). One clarification worth making up front: existing Delta Sharing clients and integrations remain compatible with OpenSharing. This is an evolution of the protocol, not a break from it, and the delta-io/delta-sharing repository continues to exist alongside the new OpenSharing-IO/OpenSharing GitHub organization. Diagram: Delta Sharing evolves into OpenSharing, which operates as an open protocol layer on GitHub plus a Databricks enterprise implementation layer, with new reach into Iceberg REST Catalog clients and on-premises or private cloud storage. A broader asset model. The original open Delta Sharing protocol centered on tables, even as Databricks-to-Databricks sharing had grown to cover more asset types. OpenSharing brings that broader model into the open specification itself and introduces a Share → Schema → Asset hierarchy that extends sharing beyond Tables to new asset types, including Volumes (directories of files in any format), Agent Skills, and AI models ( GitHub, OpenSharing ). This means a provider can package a data product that includes both the underlying tables and the AI assets built on top of them, and share the whole thing through one protocol. Diagram: OpenSharing's asset hierarchy. Table, Volume, Agent Skill, and Model are specified asset types today. Agent and Page or Glossary types are listed as community proposals still under discussion. Iceberg REST Catalog support. OpenSharing adds support for Apache Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) compatible clients, so providers can share data to any Iceberg-compatible engine, not only Delta Sharing native clients. Databricks describes this as extending the reach of open sharing to organizations standardized on Iceberg tooling ( Databricks product page ). On-premises and private cloud reach. Through the Databricks Storage Ecosystem, storage vendors can run an OpenSharing server that connects directly to Unity Catalog, so data that lives on premises or in a private cloud can be governed and shared without first migrating it ( Databricks blog ). MinIO's AIStor integration is generally available, with additional storage partners in preview or committed for later in 2026. Zero-copy credential vending stays the model. Providers don't move data to share it. The sharing server issues temporary, scoped credentials, and the server itself sits outside the data path, consistent with how Delta Sharing worked ( GitHub, OpenSharing ). New sharing capabilities. Alongside the protocol change, Databricks introduced several capabilities on top of OpenSharing: Governance moved to the Linux Foundation. OpenSharing has been contributed to the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation, where it is currently at the sandbox stage, the entry point for new projects under that foundation before they progress to incubation ( GitHub, OpenSharing and opensharing.io ). Changes to the spec go through a public proposal and review process rather than being decided unilaterally, which is the same governance pattern Delta Lake and Delta Sharing already followed as Linux Foundation projects. If you have shares, recipients, and connectors set up today, none of that goes away. OpenSharing is additive: your existing tables, connectors, and workflows continue to work, and the new asset types and capabilities are available as you choose to adopt them. Enabling OpenSharing for a Unity Catalog metastore is a configuration step, not a migration, and the same Create Share, Create Recipient, and Grant Access workflow you already know still applies to new asset types as they become available ( Databricks documentation ).
